title: Given a set of distinct positive numbers and a target, find all unique combinations that sum to the target, where each number may be reused unlimited times.
keyPoints: Backtracking subtracts each candidate from the remaining target and recurses; record when remaining hits zero
Recurse with the same index (not i + 1) to permit unlimited reuse of each candidate
Start loop at the current index to prevent reordered duplicates; fixes non-decreasing order
Prune branches where remaining goes negative; sorting enables early-break when a candidate exceeds remaining
The same template with i + 1 gives combinations without reuse; adding a consecutive-skip gives dedup for duplicate inputs
Time is exponential, bounded by the number of valid combinations times their average length
This is LeetCode 39 and a foundational backtracking pattern

s1_definition.oneliner: Subtract a chosen number from the remaining target and recurse from the same index for reuse; record at zero, prune below zero.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Combination Sum** – find every multiset of candidates, drawn with unlimited repeats, whose total equals a target.
- **Reuse rule** – recurse with the same index `i` (not `i + 1`) so a candidate can appear any number of times.
- **Deduplication** – loop starts at `start`, never going backward, which fixes non-decreasing order and prevents order-based duplicates.
- **Two base cases** – remaining equals zero means record a valid combination; remaining goes negative means prune.
- **Pruning** – sort candidates; if `candidates[i] > remaining`, break because all later candidates are larger.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India must make up an exact payout amount using denominations it can dispense in unlimited quantity, and it wants every distinct way to hit that amount. A clerk picks a denomination, subtracts it from the target, and keeps picking, allowed to pick the same denomination again. If she reaches exactly zero she has found one valid way; if she overshoots she abandons that attempt.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Combination Sum asks for every combination of distinct candidates that sums to a target, with unlimited reuse allowed. The backtracking carries a start index and a remaining target. When remaining hits zero, record the path. When it goes negative, prune. The crucial choice is recursing with the same index to permit reuse.

The start index prevents looking backward, fixing a non-decreasing order that eliminates order-based duplicates. Sorting the candidates unlocks an early-break prune: once a candidate exceeds the remaining target, all later candidates do too, so you break the loop.

At the National Bank of India, the cash dispensing module used this to enumerate every way to assemble a withdrawal from note denominations, each dispensable in unlimited quantity. The sorted-break pruning kept the search responsive even for larger amounts.

The same backtracking skeleton with a tweak to the index rule gives combinations without reuse (i + 1 instead of i), and adding a consecutive-skip handles inputs with duplicates. This makes Combination Sum a cornerstone pattern that unlocks a whole family of problems with minimal changes.

Remember one sentence: recurse with the same index for reuse, start the loop at the current index to avoid duplicates, and sort plus break for pruning.
